mcq.prompt: Your build reports `__cplusplus == 202302L`. What does that establish?
choices: That the compiler and standard library implement every C++23 feature
That std::expected is available
That `import std;` will work
Only that the compiler was invoked in C++23 language mode
mcq.explain: `__cplusplus` reports the selected language mode and nothing more; compilers and standard libraries ship individual features on their own schedules and sometimes backport them into older modes. Gate on the specific feature-test macro — `__cpp_lib_expected` for std::expected — which answers the question you actually have.

mcq.prompt: Why do feature-test macros hold dates such as `201907L` rather than being defined-or-not?
choices: To record when the vendor shipped the feature, for support purposes
So code can require a particular revision of the feature, not just its presence
Because the preprocessor cannot compare boolean macros
To let the standard deprecate a feature by lowering its value
mcq.explain: Features get revised, so `#if defined(__cpp_concepts) && __cpp_concepts >= 201907L` asks for a specific revision rather than an early partial implementation. The value is the standard's revision date, not the vendor's ship date, and it never goes backwards. Never define a reserved `__cpp_` macro yourself — an absent or older value means the implementation cannot support the path you selected.

mcq.prompt: How many times is the range expression in `for (int price : make_book())` evaluated?
choices: Once, with the result bound to a hidden `auto&&` reference
Once per iteration
Twice: once for begin and once for end
Once per element plus one final call for the end position
mcq.explain: The transformation binds the range expression's result to a hidden reference once, then obtains the beginning and ending positions once from that. Re-evaluating per iteration is what a hand-written `for (i = 0; i < f().size(); ++i)` does by accident — and is precisely the cost the range-based form removes.

mcq.prompt: How does the loop find the beginning and ending positions of its range?
choices: Always through free begin(range) and end(range) found by ADL
Always through member range.begin() and range.end()
Suitable members first; otherwise free begin/end found by argument-dependent lookup
Through std::ranges::begin only, which is why C-arrays need std::span
mcq.explain: Lookup considers suitable member `begin()`/`end()` first, and falls back to free functions found by ADL — which is how a third-party type gains range support without editing the class. The two returned types need not match: a sentinel end is normal in the C++20 iterator protocol.

mcq.prompt: `for (char c : Text{"FAST"}.view())` iterates a string_view over a temporary Text's member. What is its status?
choices: Undefined behaviour in every standard revision
Well-defined in every standard revision, because the temporary binds to the hidden auto&&
Ill-formed, because a string_view is not a range
Undefined behaviour before C++23; valid in C++23, which extends temporaries inside the range initializer
mcq.explain: Before C++23 only the outer temporary bound directly to the hidden reference was lifetime-extended, and here that outer object is the string_view — the Text died at the end of the initializer, leaving the view dangling. C++23 extends the temporaries inside the range initializer through the loop. It does not repair a function that returns a dangling reference to its by-value parameter: that parameter still dies in the callee.

mcq.prompt: What does `auto [price, quantity] = order;` actually create?
choices: Two independent variables, each copy-initialised from the corresponding member
One hidden Order object copy-initialised from order, with two names bound into it
Two references into order itself
A std::tuple<std::int64_t, int> holding copies of the members
mcq.explain: The declaration before `[` initialises one hidden object — here a copy of the whole Order — and the names are bindings into that object, not separate variables. That is why a by-value binding copies the entire record even when you read only one name, and why `auto&` instead binds the hidden object to the original.

mcq.prompt: In which order does the compiler consider the structured-binding protocols?
choices: Built-in arrays, then tuple-like via tuple_size/tuple_element/get, then eligible classes' data members
Eligible classes' data members, then tuple-like, then arrays
Tuple-like first, so a class with both members and a get() is always unpacked as a tuple
Whichever yields the requested number of names
mcq.explain: Arrays bind element-per-name, then the tuple-like protocol is tried, and only if neither applies are an eligible class's non-static data members bound in declaration order. The priority matters for a class that opts into tuple_size: it is then unpacked as a tuple even though it also has members — but that only happens because the tuple-like check comes after arrays and before members, not because it comes first.

mcq.prompt: After `auto& [live_price, live_quantity] = order;`, what is `decltype(live_quantity)` where `order.quantity` is an int?
choices: int&, matching the reference in the declaration
const int, because bindings are immutable
int — the declared member type — even though assigning through the binding modifies order
It is ill-formed: decltype may not be applied to a binding name
mcq.explain: A binding name is not a reference variable; `decltype` on it yields the referenced member's declared type, so `int`, even though the binding writes through to `order`. Parenthesise it — `decltype((live_quantity))` — and the ordinary expression rules apply, giving a reference type. This mirrors the `decltype(x)` versus `decltype((x))` distinction exactly.

mcq.prompt: A struct declares `auto operator<=>(const Price&) const = default;` and nothing else. Which expressions work?
choices: Only <, >, <= and >=; equality must still be written by hand
Only <=> itself; the relational operators must be written by hand
Only == and !=
<, >, <=, >=, == and != all work
mcq.explain: The compiler rewrites `bid < ask` as `(bid <=> ask) < 0`, and a *defaulted* `<=>` also implicitly declares a matching defaulted `operator==` — so equality comes along too. The catch is that a hand-written `<=>` does not: if you write the spaceship yourself, you must define `operator==` as well.

mcq.prompt: What is the comparison category of a defaulted `<=>` on a struct whose only member is a double?
choices: std::strong_ordering, because double has a total order over its representations
std::partial_ordering, because NaN is unordered with everything
std::weak_ordering, because -0.0 and +0.0 compare equal
It is ill-formed; floating-point members cannot be defaulted
mcq.explain: Built-in floating-point comparison yields `std::partial_ordering` because NaN is unordered against every value including itself, and the defaulted operator inherits the weakest member category. That is a real hazard: feeding such values to an ordered container breaks its strict-weak-ordering requirement. Weak ordering is for equivalent-but-distinguishable values, such as case-folded symbols.

mcq.prompt: Why does the standard keep `operator==` separate rather than always deriving it from `<=>`?
choices: Because equality can often be decided faster than a full ordering — a length check rejects most string pairs immediately
Because <=> cannot be constexpr
Because == must be a member while <=> must be a free function
Because equality has to work for types with no ordering, which <=> cannot express
mcq.explain: Deriving `==` from a full three-way comparison would throw away cheap shortcuts: two strings of different lengths are unequal without inspecting a character. Both operators can be members or friends and both can be constexpr; a type may also default `==` alone when it has no meaningful order.

mcq.prompt: Which statement about `constexpr` on a function is accurate?
choices: Every call is evaluated at compile time
It is a hint the optimizer may ignore
It permits use in constant expressions; an ordinary call may still execute at runtime
It implies the function is inline and has internal linkage
mcq.explain: `constexpr` says the function is *permitted* in a constant expression and must be evaluated at compile time where one is required — initialising a `constexpr` variable or checking a `static_assert`. Called with runtime arguments it is an ordinary function. `consteval` is the keyword for 'compile time or it is an error'.

mcq.prompt: `constexpr int invalid = values[3];` indexes a two-element constexpr array. What happens?
choices: It compiles, and reading `invalid` at runtime is undefined behaviour
It compiles and yields an unspecified value
It compiles with a warning under -Warray-bounds
It fails to compile: undefined behaviour is rejected during required constant evaluation
mcq.explain: A constant expression may not contain undefined behaviour, so out-of-bounds reads, signed overflow and invalid shifts are compile errors on executed constant-evaluation paths — constant evaluation acts as a build-time sanitizer with no runtime cost. Index the same array with a runtime variable and you get ordinary, undiagnosed undefined behaviour instead.

mcq.prompt: What does `constinit int sequence_start = compute_start();` guarantee?
choices: That sequence_start is const and cannot be modified after initialisation
That the initialisation happens at compile time, while the object remains mutable
That the object is initialised before any other translation unit's statics
That every later write to the object is also a constant expression
mcq.explain: `constinit` constrains initialisation only: the object must be constant-initialised, so the cross-translation-unit dynamic-initialisation ordering hazard disappears and there is no first-use guard — but the object is still writable, which is exactly the point for mutable static state. A `constexpr` variable is the one that is also `const`.

mcq.prompt: For `template<class Self> decltype(auto) price(this Self&& self)`, what is `Self` deduced as when the member is called on a non-const lvalue Quote?
choices: Quote&
Quote
Quote&&
const Quote&
mcq.explain: The explicit object parameter is deduced exactly like any other forwarding reference, so an lvalue argument deduces an lvalue-reference type and the parameter collapses to `Quote&`. Calling on a `const` object deduces `const Quote&` and on a temporary deduces `Quote` — which is how one function replaces an overload set that differed only in object qualification.

mcq.prompt: Which restriction applies to a member function with an explicit object parameter?
choices: It must be a template
It may not be const-qualified
It has no implicit `this`, and it cannot be virtual
It may not have any additional parameters
mcq.explain: The object is now a named parameter, so `this` is not available and every member must be reached through `self`; such a function also cannot be `virtual`. It need not be a template — `Price scaled(this Price self, std::int64_t factor)` takes the object by value and has an ordinary extra parameter.

mcq.prompt: Which of these does `export` in a module interface unit actually do?
choices: Guarantees a stable binary ABI for the exported entity
Hides the layout of exported class types from importers
Makes the entity immune to ordinary source-compatibility concerns
Makes the declaration visible to translation units that import the module
mcq.explain: `export` controls source visibility to importers and nothing else. Modules change how declarations reach a translation unit, not what those declarations mean — an exported struct's layout is as visible and as fragile as it ever was, and changing it still breaks compatibility with already-compiled callers.

mcq.prompt: A header defined `#define ENABLE_TRACING 1`. The team replaces the `#include` with an `import` of the equivalent module. What happens to the macro?
choices: It is exported with the rest of the module's interface
It does not cross the import boundary, so code depending on it breaks
It becomes visible only inside the module's implementation units
It is replaced by a compiler-generated constexpr variable of the same name
mcq.explain: Macros are a preprocessing-time phenomenon and do not cross an import boundary at all — that macro isolation is one of the costs modules were designed to remove, and it is also the migration hazard. Configuration that used to arrive via a header macro must become a real declaration, a build-system definition, or a compiler flag.

mcq.prompt: How does `[[assume(expr)]]` differ from a contract precondition?
choices: It is never checked; reaching it with a false expr is undefined behaviour, whereas a contract is evaluated under the selected semantic
It is checked in debug builds and removed under NDEBUG, like assert
It always terminates on a false expression
It is a runtime check that the optimizer may not exploit
mcq.explain: `[[assume(expr)]]` is a promise to the optimizer, not a check: if the expression would be false, the program has undefined behaviour and the compiler is entitled to have optimised on that basis. A contract's `pre` can be ignored, observed through the violation handler, or enforced by terminating, according to the selected mode. `assert` is the NDEBUG-controlled macro.

mcq.section: Static reflection **(C++26)** and the bridge to Part V
mcq.prompt: What is the intended payoff of static reflection for wire-format code?
choices: Runtime inspection of object layout through a metadata table in the binary
Automatic ABI stability across compiler versions
Compile-time enumeration of a struct's members, removing hand-maintained parallel macro lists and code generators
Elimination of the need to define comparison operators
mcq.explain: Reflection is a compile-time facility: `^^T` yields a reflection value that consteval code can inspect, and a splice turns a reflected entity back into code — so a serializer can enumerate members from the struct itself instead of from a macro list that drifts. It adds no runtime metadata, and it makes no ABI promises. Treat the syntax as a C++26 preview, not shipping guidance.

reading.explain: Two independent facts, one per number. The range expression is evaluated exactly once — the desugaring binds `auto&& hidden = active_terrain();` before the loop and obtains the endpoints once — so `lookups` is 1, not 3. The element declaration is a separate decision: `auto cell` copies each element, so `cell.height *= 10` scales three copies that are then discarded. The heights are still 1, 2, 3 when the second loop adds one to each through `auto&`, giving 2 + 3 + 4 = 9. Expecting 39 is reading the first loop as if it had been written `auto&`; expecting 3 lookups is the mirror error of assuming a range expression is re-evaluated per iteration.

`auto [w, h] = extent;` does not initialise two variables — it creates one hidden `Extent` object, copy-initialised from `extent`, and introduces two names bound into it. Copying that hidden object copies both members, so the counter reads 2 even before either name is used. `auto& [...]` binds the hidden object to the existing lvalue instead: no copy at all, the counter is still 2, and writing through `live_width` reaches `extent.width`, which is why the third value is 9. The last check is the chapter's note about `decltype`: a binding's declared type is the member type, `Counted`, not `Counted&`, even though assigning through it mutates the original — `decltype((live_width))` follows ordinary expression rules and would give the reference. The trap is expecting 1 copy: the declaration before `[` initialises the whole object, however few names you go on to read.

A defaulted `<=>` compares members lexicographically in *declaration* order, so representation order silently becomes comparison order. `Stored` lists `patch` first, and version 1.0.9 against 2.0.0 therefore compares 9 against 0 and stops: 1.0.9 is reported as the *greater* version, so `older_stored < newer_stored` is false. `Declared` lists the same three fields major-first and answers true. Both are `strong_ordering`, because all the members are integral — the category comes from the members, and a `double` member would have produced `partial_ordering` instead. The lesson is the one the chapter states directly: if business ordering differs from storage order, write the spaceship out rather than rearranging members for semantics.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: `constinit` is a *requirement*, not a request: the object must be constant-initialised, and `detect_transitions()` is an ordinary function, so its call is not a constant expression and the initialisation would have to be dynamic. The compiler rejects it. Without `constinit` this compiles and prints 12, and that is exactly the situation the keyword exists to forbid — the object would then be dynamically initialised at namespace scope, and any other translation unit's dynamic initialiser that reads it might run first and see a zero. Marking the function `constexpr` is the fix; note also what `constinit` does not do, which is make the object const. It constrains initialisation and leaves the object mutable.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: The member is written correctly, parentheses included, and that is what creates the hazard. For the lvalue `stored`, `Self` is deduced as `Reading&` and the return type is `int&`, so `live += 5` really does update the object. For the prvalue `Reading{240}`, `Self` is `Reading` and the return type is `int&&` — a reference to a member of a temporary. A reference returned *from a function* is never lifetime-extended, so the temporary is destroyed at the end of that full-expression and `sampled` dangles immediately; AddressSanitizer reports stack-use-after-scope on the next line. The tempting reading is that binding the result to `int&&` extends the temporary the way `const T& r = T{}` does; it extends nothing here, because what is bound is the function's return value, not the temporary itself. Take the value by copy, or keep the object alive in a named variable.

`origin` is one function that observes how it is being evaluated. Initialising `folded`, a `constexpr` variable, requires a constant expression, so the `if consteval` branch is taken and the value is 1. `recorded` is `constinit`, which also *requires* constant initialisation — same branch, same 1. The call inside `main` is an ordinary runtime call with no constant expression required of it, so the else branch runs and prints 2. That is the whole distinction the table draws: `constexpr` means permitted in a constant expression, not evaluated in one, and `constinit` constrains initialisation while leaving the object mutable. Expecting `1 1 1` assumes a `constexpr` function always folds; expecting `2 2 2` forgets that `constexpr` and `constinit` variables force the compile-time path.

writing.prompt: Write a logging fragment that must compile on a toolchain missing `std::print` and on one missing explicit object parameters, and must present the same call site either way. Gate each facility on the right macro, request a specific revision where the feature has one, and say in a comment why a `__cplusplus` test would not do the job.
checklist: Includes <version> before testing a library macro, and notes that a language macro needs no header
Tests __cpp_lib_print and __cpp_explicit_this_parameter, never __cplusplus or a compiler version
The feature-specific header is included only inside the branch that uses it
At least one gate compares against a revision date rather than testing for definedness alone
Both branches present the same interface, so the call site below is written once
writing.notes: The macros carry dates rather than booleans precisely so that code can ask for a revision — an implementation that shipped an early version of a feature defines the macro with an older value, and `#ifdef` alone would select a path it cannot support. Note also which side each macro comes from: `__cpp_lib_*` is published by the standard library through `<version>` or the feature's own header, while `__cpp_*` comes from the compiler and is available with no include at all. Never define a reserved `__cpp_` macro yourself.

writing.prompt: Write a loop that counts a character in the text of a document obtained from a function with an observable side effect. The contract: the function must run exactly once per loop no matter how long the text is, no element may be copied, and the loop must remain valid when iterating a view of a temporary. Write the desugared form beside it to prove the first property, and add the three element-declaration variants with a note on when each is right.
checklist: The desugared form binds the range expression once to an `auto&&` and obtains both endpoints before the loop
The side-effect counter demonstrates one evaluation per loop, not one per element
The reading loop uses a reference element declaration so nothing is copied
A loop over a view of a temporary is present, with a comment that C++23 extends the temporaries in the range initialiser and that this was undefined behaviour before
The `auto`, `auto&` and `const auto&` variants each carry a comment saying when to use them
writing.notes: The C++23 extension covers temporaries created inside the range initialiser, and it is worth being precise about what it does not repair: a function that returns a reference or a view into its own by-value parameter still dangles, because that parameter dies in the callee and was never a temporary of the loop's full-expression. The rule from Chapter 5 still applies — know which object owns the elements you are iterating.

writing.prompt: Make `auto [width, height] = box;` compile for a class whose data members are private, then use structured bindings for two more shapes: unpacking a tuple-returning function, and incrementing every value in a `std::map` in place. Explain in comments what the declaration before `[` controls and why the map loop uses the binding form it does.
checklist: The private class opts into the tuple-like protocol with std::tuple_size, std::tuple_element and a get
A tuple-returning function is unpacked with a structured binding
The map loop uses a reference binding so the increment reaches the container
A comment states that the declaration before `[` initialises one hidden object and the names bind into it
A comment notes that a by-value binding copies the whole entry even when one name is written
writing.notes: The three protocols are tried in a fixed order — built-in array, then tuple-like, then binding the non-static data members — and the third is unavailable here because the members are private, which is exactly why opting into the second is worth the boilerplate. Note that `get` can be a member template or a free function found by ADL; the specialisations of `tuple_size` and `tuple_element` must be in namespace `std`. Bindings still cannot nest patterns or skip elements; packs such as `auto [first, ...rest]` are a C++26 preview.

writing.prompt: A `Version` record stores its fields patch, minor, major in that order because the wire format says so, but must compare major-first. A `Tag` must compare case-insensitively. Write both types so each is usable as a `std::set` key, and say in comments why defaulting is wrong for the first and why the second cannot be a strong ordering.
checklist: Version writes its spaceship explicitly rather than reordering members, with a comment that defaulting compares in declaration order
Version and Tag each define operator== explicitly, with a comment that a hand-written <=> declares no equality
Tag's operator<=> returns std::weak_ordering, with a comment explaining that case-folded equivalence is not substitutability
Both types are exercised as std::set keys
A comment notes that a defaulted <=> over a double member would yield partial_ordering and break an ordered container
writing.notes: Rearranging the members to make defaulting produce the right answer is the tempting shortcut, and it changes the layout of a type whose layout is fixed by the wire format — the comparison is the thing that should bend. Note the early-exit shape of the explicit version: it is the same memberwise lexicographic comparison the compiler would have generated, just over a different member order. Equality stays separate from ordering throughout because implementations can usually decide it faster, such as by rejecting strings of different lengths first.

writing.prompt: Build a string-scanner state machine whose transition table is computed by the compiler and shipped in read-only data. Use all four facilities: a `constexpr` transition function and table checked by `static_assert`, a `consteval` validator that makes an unwanted input a build error, a `constinit` mutable counter, and `if consteval` so one function takes a different path during constant evaluation. Comment each with what it guarantees and what it does not.
checklist: The table is produced by a constexpr function and stored in an inline constexpr variable, with at least two static_asserts checking entries
The consteval function is used only in a constant-expression context and rejects bad input at compile time
The constinit object is written to at run time, demonstrating that it is not const
if consteval selects a different path without template machinery, and a static_assert pins the compile-time answer
Comments distinguish 'may run at compile time', 'must run at compile time' and 'must be initialised at compile time'
writing.notes: The `throw` inside the consteval validator is not a runtime error path — a throw reached during required constant evaluation is simply not a constant expression, so it becomes a compile error with the message attached. That is the general shape of the facility: constant evaluation rejects executed undefined behaviour at build time, so out-of-range table indices and overflow fail the build instead of becoming runtime UB. The table itself is the payoff described in the Latency Lens — it lands in read-only data instead of being generated during startup, and each scan step is one indexed load.

writing.prompt: Replace four accessor overloads — `&`, `const&`, `&&`, `const&&` — with a single explicit-object member whose result keeps the const-ness and value category of the object it was called on. Prove the three interesting cases with `static_assert`, add a by-value explicit object parameter for a small type, and name the two restrictions such members carry.
checklist: The replacement uses `template<class Self>` with `this Self&& self` and `decltype(auto)`
The returned member access is parenthesised, with a comment explaining what the unparenthesised form would return and why that is wrong
static_asserts check that the lvalue, const lvalue and rvalue cases yield the matching reference types
Every member access inside goes through self, and a by-value explicit object parameter is also demonstrated
Comments name both restrictions: no implicit this, and such a member cannot be virtual
writing.notes: The parentheses are the part worth rehearsing. `decltype(auto)` applies `decltype` rules to the return expression, and `decltype` of an unparenthesised member access reports the member's *declared* type — so the unparenthesised version returns `std::string` by value from every instantiation, compiles cleanly, and silently deletes the whole point of the member. Parenthesised, `decltype` sees an lvalue or xvalue expression and yields `std::string&`, `const std::string&` or `std::string&&`. It is the same rule as `decltype((quantity))` from Chapter 2. Note the lifetime consequence too: a caller that binds the rvalue result gets a reference into a temporary that dies at the end of the full-expression.
